findings.title: Unauthenticated RCE via eval() on caller-supplied filter expression
findings.why: applyFilterExpression passes the caller-controlled `expression` field directly to Python's eval() with no sandboxing or allowlist. Any authenticated caller (or unauthenticated if current_user_id returns None) can POST to /notes/filter with an expression such as `__import__('os').system('...')` and execute arbitrary OS commands as the server process. The PR description frames this as intentional ('power users can write whatever they want'), making it a design-level RCE, not just an implementation slip.
findings.evidence: return [n for n in notes if eval(expression)]
findings.fix: Replace eval() with a safe predicate DSL. At minimum, parse the expression into an AST, whitelist only comparison/boolean node types, and evaluate against note fields in a restricted namespace — never call eval() or exec() on network-supplied input.

findings.title: SQL injection in search_notes via f-string query interpolation
findings.why: The previously parameterised query was replaced with a raw f-string that embeds both `user_id` and `query` directly into SQL. An attacker controlling either value (query via ?q=, user_id via a crafted token — see SEC-3) can inject arbitrary SQL, dump the entire database, or modify/delete rows. The PR description explicitly states this was done to 'support the % wildcard', confirming the change was intentional.
findings.evidence: sql = f"SELECT id, title, body FROM notes WHERE user_id = {user_id} AND title LIKE '%{query}%'"
findings.fix: Restore parameterised queries: cur.execute("SELECT id, title, body FROM notes WHERE user_id = ? AND title LIKE ?", (user_id, "%" + query + "%")). To support literal % wildcards, escape them before constructing the parameter value rather than interpolating into SQL.

findings.title: Token auth is a no-op — any user_id accepted without signature verification
findings.why: current_user_id splits the token on '.' and returns int(parts[1]) with zero cryptographic verification. The SHA-1 prefix (parts[0]) is never checked. An attacker can forge a token of the form 'anything.<victim_user_id>' and impersonate any user. Because this function now gates /notes/search and /notes/create, the entire identity model for those endpoints is bypassed.
findings.fix: Verify the signature before trusting the user_id. Recompute HMAC-SHA256(user_id + "|" + timestamp, JWT_SECRET) and compare with constant-time comparison. Also verify the timestamp is within the allowed window (24 h). Reject the token if either check fails.

findings.title: SQL injection in delete_note via f-string note_id interpolation
findings.why: delete_note constructs the DELETE statement by interpolating note_id directly into an f-string. Although Flask's <int:note_id> route converter enforces an integer at the HTTP layer, the function itself accepts any value and is called from application code. A future internal caller or a bypass of the route layer would allow arbitrary SQL. The bare except clause also silently suppresses all database errors, masking injection attempts.
findings.fix: Use a parameterised statement: cur.execute("DELETE FROM notes WHERE id = ?", (note_id,)). Remove the bare except/pass block so database errors are surfaced.

findings.title: Hardcoded admin bypass token 'letmein-admin' grants unrestricted note deletion
findings.why: ADMIN_BYPASS_TOKEN = "letmein-admin" is committed in plaintext. Anyone who reads the source code (public repo, leaked repo, insider) can send X-Admin-Token: letmein-admin and delete any note in the system. The secret is trivially guessable even without code access. This is the sole guard on the DELETE /notes/<id> endpoint.
findings.fix: Remove the hardcoded value. Load admin credentials exclusively from an environment variable or secrets manager: ADMIN_BYPASS_TOKEN = os.environ['ADMIN_BYPASS_TOKEN']. Rotate the value immediately if this commit is or was public.

findings.title: Full Python traceback returned to caller on exception in /notes/filter
findings.why: Any exception from applyFilterExpression (including a deliberately triggered one) causes traceback.format_exc() to be serialised into the JSON response body. This leaks full server-side stack traces, file system paths, Python interpreter internals, and potentially fragments of application data to external callers. An attacker can exploit this to map the application's internals before escalating to RCE (SEC-1).
findings.fix: Log the traceback server-side (e.g. app.logger.exception(e)) and return only a generic message to the caller: return jsonify({"error": "internal server error"}), 500.

findings.title: Tokens never expire — issued timestamp is never validated by current_user_id
findings.why: issue_token embeds a Unix timestamp in the token payload and its docstring claims '24 hours' validity. current_user_id never parses or checks the timestamp, so every token is permanently valid. A stolen or leaked token cannot be invalidated by time. Combined with the missing signature verification (SEC-3), this makes credential revocation impossible without a database-level token blocklist.
findings.evidence:
raw = str(user_id) + "|" + str(int(time.time())) + "|" + JWT_SECRET
    return hashlib.sha1(raw.encode()).hexdigest() + "." + str(user_id)
findings.fix: After fixing SEC-3, include the timestamp in parts[1] (e.g. 'sig.userid.issued_at'), parse it in current_user_id, and reject tokens where time.time() - issued_at > 86400.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 — trivially crackable via rainbow tables
findings.why: hash_password uses hashlib.md5 with no salt. MD5 is cryptographically broken and entire precomputed rainbow tables exist for common passwords. This function was pre-existing but is now actively exercised via the /auth/register endpoint wired in this PR, elevating it from latent to actively exploitable. All stored password hashes are vulnerable to offline cracking if the database is compromised.
findings.fix: Replace with bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2: import bcrypt; return bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt()). Update verify_password accordingly and plan a migration of existing hashes.

findings.title: Pre-existing hardcoded JWT_SECRET now actively used for token signing
findings.why: JWT_SECRET was already hardcoded before this PR. This PR activates it: issue_token now uses it as the only signing material for user tokens, and current_user_id (SEC-3) does not verify it. Even if SEC-3 is fixed and signatures are verified, the secret is committed to version control and therefore known to anyone with repo access, making all issued tokens forgeable.
findings.fix: Load from environment: JWT_SECRET = os.environ['JWT_SECRET']. Rotate the value and invalidate all outstanding tokens after deployment.
